routes.description: Establish that biblical truth is properly assessed through genre, revelation, human testimony, and established interpretive tradition, and that textual variation or morally difficult passages need not defeat its historical, theological, moral, or revelatory claims.
routes.successCriteria: Connect an account of revelation and human transmission to affirmative historical or cosmological support, while explaining why apparent contradictions and difficult moral texts do not undermine the Bible's governing truth claims.

motionBridge.description: Show that the Bible remains true in its governing revelatory and theological purpose while retaining sufficient historical and moral credibility across its diverse genres.

centralBridges.description: Define biblical truth through revelation, genre, authorial purpose, and human expression rather than requiring uniform literal or scientific precision.
Establish that cumulative testimony and external corroboration support the historical credibility of the biblical narratives despite nonidentical details.
Explain morally troubling texts through moral development, fulfillment, and the established interpretive practice of living Christian communities.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use claimed convergence between Genesis and later cosmological inquiry as supporting evidence for revelation.
Distinguish ordinary testimonial variation from central falsification and explain why miraculous claims remain possible within the asserted theology.

routes.description: Establish that each biblical claim must meet standards appropriate to its genre and that historical contradictions, theological reshaping, selective evidential methods, and morally troubling divine commands undermine the Bible's asserted forms of truth.
routes.successCriteria: Demonstrate that the principal historical, revelatory, and moral claims face unresolved contradictions or counterexamples that cannot be answered merely by invoking genre, possibility, later tradition, or beneficial reception.

motionBridge.description: Show that contradictions and morally troubling texts materially undermine the Bible's historical, moral, theological, allegorical, or revelatory truth claims.

centralBridges.description: Separate the Bible's genres and require attempted historical reports, moral teachings, and allegories to satisfy the standards appropriate to each claim.
Show that Gospel discrepancies, textual development, and theological reshaping reduce confidence in the narratives used to support central Christian events.
Show that divinely authorized killing and slavery remain incompatible with asserted biblical moral authority despite later reinterpretation or moral development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Require consistent treatment of favorable and unfavorable scientific, archaeological, and textual details when inferring revelation or reliability.
Distinguish the logical possibility of miracles from evidence that specifically biblical miracle reports occurred.

sections.title: Standards of Truth, Genre, and Revelation
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the governing standards for evaluating a diverse scriptural library, including the roles of authorial purpose, human expression, revelation, allegory, and inherited interpretation.

sections.title: Gospel Historicity, Contradictions, and Transmission
sections.rationale: The historical reliability of the Gospels is a principal motion-level clash because discrepancies, editorial development, cumulative testimony, and theological shaping bear directly on central Christian events.

sections.title: Cosmology, Archaeological Corroboration, and Miracles
sections.rationale: Affirmative appeals to scientific anticipation, archaeological detail, and miraculous possibility must be weighed against alternative explanations and limits on what mundane corroboration can establish.

sections.title: Divine Violence and Biblical Moral Authority
sections.rationale: Commands involving conquest and the killing of noncombatants create a direct test of claimed divine moral authority and of whether development, fulfillment, or interpretive tradition resolves difficult texts.

sections.title: Slavery, Moral Development, and Abolitionist Reception
sections.rationale: Biblical slave laws, later teachings, abolitionist use, and communal interpretation test whether the canon presents coherent moral development or contains unresolved moral instability.

routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is reasonable through a cumulative historical inference from Jesus' death, the reported empty tomb and appearances, witness transformations, early proclamation, and comparison with rival explanations.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if its principal historical claims are adequately supported, bodily resurrection explains their conjunction better than the live alternatives, and the evidential standard permits supernatural causation to be inferred without first assuming it.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative historical and explanatory case to the conclusion that belief in Jesus' bodily resurrection is epistemically reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish the material historical data concerning death, burial or the empty tomb, reported appearances, conversions, and early resurrection proclamation.
Show that bodily resurrection has greater explanatory scope and power than conspiracy, hallucination, legend, error, or combinations of natural alternatives.
Show that the event's religious context and the failure of competing explanations warrant identifying the resurrection as divine action.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the historical sources through their asserted earliness, multiplicity, local detail, cultural fit, archaeology, and relevant scholarly agreement.
Defend ordinary cumulative historical reasoning against standards alleged to exclude extraordinary conclusions categorically or generate an evidential regress.

routes.description: Establish that belief in Jesus' resurrection is unreasonable because transmitted reports, disputed historical premises, and background compatibility do not provide sufficient warrant for either the event or its supernatural cause.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available sources do not adequately establish the material premises, ordinary explanations or unresolved uncertainty remain live, or the evidence fails to meet the burden appropriate to an extraordinary supernatural conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Connect the insufficiency and underdetermination of the available evidence to withholding belief in bodily resurrection as the reasonable position.

centralBridges.description: Show that late, dependent, disputed, or second- and third-hand reports cannot securely establish the proposed resurrection facts.
Show that sincerity, movement growth, accurate background details, and reported experiences remain compatible with legend, error, transmission, or unknown causes.
Require evidence not only that an unusual event occurred but also that resurrection was possible and that supernatural or divine causation produced it.
Apply an evidential burden proportionate to the extraordinariness and low background plausibility of bodily resurrection.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish reports, sincere beliefs, and incidental historical accuracy from independent support for the resurrection proposition itself.
Defend suspension of judgment without requiring a complete rival reconstruction or a claim that resurrection is impossible.

sections.title: Historical facts and source reliability
sections.rationale: The cumulative inference depends on whether death, burial, the empty tomb, appearances, conversions, and early proclamation are established by sufficiently early, independent, consistent, and reliable sources.

sections.title: Testimony, sincerity, and corroboration
sections.rationale: The parties dispute what reported experiences, costly commitment, local knowledge, archaeology, and accurate background details can establish about the central resurrection claims.

sections.title: Resurrection and rival explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns substantially on whether resurrection explains the proposed historical data better than legend, deception, hallucination, error, transmission, combined alternatives, or unresolved uncertainty.

sections.title: Event evidence and supernatural causation
sections.rationale: Evidence for an unusual return to life and evidence that God caused a bodily resurrection are distinct inferential questions whose connection is necessary to the motion.

sections.title: Extraordinary claims and evidential burden
sections.rationale: The appropriate relationship among prior plausibility, extraordinary claims, proportional evidence, and historical inference determines what support reasonable belief requires.

sections.title: Reasonable belief and suspension of judgment
sections.rationale: The ultimate burden requires deciding whether the cumulative case warrants belief or whether remaining evidential uncertainty makes suspension of judgment the justified motion-level conclusion.

routes.description: Establish that Christian fellowship and scientific vocation can remain intact while confidence in evolutionary explanations is limited by unresolved causal mechanisms in major biological transitions, origins, and extrapolations beyond observed change.
routes.successCriteria: Show that accepting observable adaptation and interpretive flexibility does not warrant treating proposed mechanisms for body-plan innovation, origins chemistry, or other large-scale transitions as established when their causal sufficiency remains unresolved.

motionBridge.description: Connect unresolved causal mechanisms in the motion's disputed domains to a principled limit on warranted evolutionary confidence without making origins disagreement a test of Christian faith.

centralBridges.description: Require testable causal accounts rather than appeals to unknown biological laws or compressed transition narratives.
Distinguish observed, mechanistically tractable small-scale change from claims about major anatomical and genomic innovation.
Explain why unresolved chemistry and unsupported transition mechanisms materially bear on claims concerning origins and body plans.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test agency-based interpretations against inheritance, selection, and horizontal-transfer explanations where those alternatives apply.
Ground Christian unity and scientific participation in shared faith while allowing multiple interpretations of disputed scriptural and scientific questions.

routes.description: Establish that Christian faith can accommodate a bounded contemporary evolutionary framework enriched by organismal agency, cognition, reciprocal environmental effects, inheritance, and structural principles, despite unresolved mechanisms and limits concerning origins and human uniqueness.
routes.successCriteria: Show that mechanistic incompleteness does not nullify the general evolutionary framework, while defining its proper boundaries and connecting modern biological concepts and scriptural interpretation to a non-hostile relationship between science and Christian faith.

motionBridge.description: Integrate a bounded evolutionary account with Christian commitments by identifying its biological basis, acknowledged limits, and implications for fellowship and scientific vocation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that living systems exhibit environmentally responsive agency or cognition relevant to a non-purely-blind account of evolutionary change.
Explain how niche construction, natural genetic engineering, inheritance, convergence, or structural constraints expand the mutation-selection picture.
Justify retaining a general evolutionary framework despite unresolved mechanisms while avoiding unsupported claims about specific transitions.
Separate biological evolution from claims about life's origin and uniquely human morality, creativity, or spiritual significance.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Relate accurate inheritance and population change to a permissible reading of scriptural language about reproduction according to kind.
Place scientific disagreement within shared Christian identity and preserve space for dialogue and participation in science.

sections.title: Agency, Cognition, and Genome-Directed Adaptation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether organismal sensing, memory, anticipation, niche construction, and genome modification materially broaden evolutionary explanation or remain accountable to inheritance-and-selection alternatives.

sections.title: Causal Mechanisms and Confidence in the Evolutionary Framework
sections.rationale: The debate centrally turns on whether unknown laws and incomplete mechanisms can coexist with justified acceptance of a general framework, or whether they make broad evolutionary narratives exceed their causal support.

sections.title: Body Plans, Genome Duplication, and Extrapolation Across Scale
sections.rationale: Major anatomical innovation provides the principal test of whether mechanisms associated with mutation, inheritance, and genome duplication can bridge the gap between observed small changes and large evolutionary transitions.

sections.title: Origins, Human Uniqueness, and the Limits of Evolution's Domain
sections.rationale: The proper scope of evolutionary explanation depends on separating biological diversification from the origin of life and from disputed genetic accounts of morality, creativity, behavior, and distinctively human qualities.

sections.title: Scriptural Interpretation, Christian Fellowship, and Scientific Vocation
sections.rationale: Reconciliation also requires an account of how Christians may interpret difficult texts, disagree about origins without salvific division, and participate in science while maintaining shared religious commitments.

routes.description: Establish that libertarian sourcehood remains coherent under non-causal determination and that Bradleyan idealism accommodates agency, normativity, feeling, and inquiry without reducing reality to natural-scientific description.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by distinguishing logical determination from causal constraint, preserving meaningful alternatives and agential influence, and showing that Bradleyan idealism explains experiential and normative dimensions that reductive naturalism or pragmatic reconstruction leaves incomplete.

motionBridge.description: Show that libertarian agency joined to Bradleyan idealism answers determinist and naturalist pressures more comprehensively than compatibilist pragmatism.

centralBridges.description: Establish agential sourcehood and alternative possibility without requiring an objectively branching future or confusing logical implication with causal control.
Explain how reasoning and deliberation remain answerable to normative standards rather than becoming merely compelled psychological sequences.
Show why an adequate metaphysics must integrate scientific truth with agency, feeling, value, and experience instead of treating scientific description as exhaustive.
Ground the intelligibility and direction of inquiry in a real idealist completion joining knower and known, not solely in a useful regulative practice.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Demonstrate that indeterminacy, top-down constraint, or level-relative explanation can make libertarian alternatives coherent even within physicalist models.
Specify experiential, operational, and intellectual constraints that prevent idealist truth from becoming arbitrary or voluntarily constructed.

routes.description: Establish that non-causal determinism preserves the practical distinctions constituting free agency and that naturalistically acceptable, experience-centered pragmatism captures inquiry and progress without Bradleyan metaphysical commitments.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by showing that fixed laws and past conditions still pressure libertarian alternatives, that functional freedom supports deliberative and responsibility practices, and that pragmatic standards explain experience and inquiry without requiring an independently real absolute.

motionBridge.description: Show that compatibilist pragmatism answers the relevant determinist and naturalist pressures without the additional modal and metaphysical commitments of libertarian idealism.

centralBridges.description: Maintain the fixed-past challenge by distinguishing broad possible-world variation from the ability to act otherwise with the actual past and laws held fixed.
Define freedom through action-guiding distinctions involving reasons-responsiveness, coercion, prediction, incentives, praise, and blame under determinism.
Account for experience as inquiry's subject matter and physical objects as experiential models without inferring anti-naturalism or conscious control of reality.
Supply constrained standards for intellectual, moral, and aesthetic progress while testing whether a real Bradleyan absolute adds necessary explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate predictability from causal puppeteering while identifying the pressure complete external predictability places on libertarian branching.
Test whether an inaccessible unstructured feeling can support Bradleyan metaphysics when reflective perception is already categorically structured.

sections.title: Determinism, Alternative Possibilities, and Sourcehood
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal modal clash over fixed pasts and laws, branching possibilities, logical determination, causal control, and whether agents can remain genuine sources.

sections.title: Normative Reasoning and Practical Freedom
sections.rationale: This issue connects the alleged self-undermining consequences of compelled reasoning with the compatibilist account of freedom through deliberation, responsibility, and socially useful distinctions.

sections.title: Naturalism, Reduction, and Experience
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether scientific explanation exhausts reality or whether experience, agency, feeling, morality, and aesthetics require the broader resources claimed for Bradleyan idealism.

sections.title: Idealist Truth, Feeling, and Perceptual Structure
sections.rationale: This issue tests how idealism constrains truth, whether precognitive feeling can ground thought, and whether unavoidable categorization supports or pressures Bradley's account of experience.

sections.title: The Absolute, Inquiry, and Pragmatic Standards
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether inquiry presupposes a genuinely real idealist completion or only a regulative commitment to progress, and what standards prevent either reductionism or unrestricted metaphysical admission.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Causal determinism threatens rational normativity because beliefs and inferences that are merely caused cannot remain answerable to independent standards of correct reasoning.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with Hawkins accepting Folley's question and develops a sustained first-person response about determinism and normativity.

response.rationale: This is a constructive statement of the pro side's central normativity challenge and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed responsivenessWithinClass values (86 and 82); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but the move shifts quickly from causal determination to beliefs being merely caused without specifying which accounts of rational answerability are excluded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The self-defeat conclusion is stronger than the supplied premise because causal production alone is not shown to eliminate truth-sensitive or norm-governed inference.

charity.alternative: A determinist can treat causal reasoning processes as truth-sensitive and responsive to logical norms.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must show why causal realization precludes normative answerability rather than merely accompanying it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference depends on an unsupported transition from being causally produced to being unable to answer to independent rational standards.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt invokes a recognized self-defeat line but supplies neither a developed warrant nor comparison with truth-tracking deterministic accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the indispensable pro normativity bridge and states the consequence for rational endorsement of determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed representationalCharity values (61 and 62); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

moves.evidenceBasis: Hawkins distinguishes correct or ought-governed reasoning from merely actual reasoning and says causal determinism would make belief in determinism itself merely caused.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins

routes.description: Establish Christian theism as the necessary worldview-level ground of logic, mathematics, knowledge, evidence, and intelligible reality, while showing that the proposed naturalistic foundation cannot account for their universal and necessary scope.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if necessary truths and the conditions of evidence are shown to require an absolute mind identified within Christian theism, and if immediate self-experience or reality alone cannot bridge subjective certainty to universally normative intelligibility.

motionBridge.description: Connect the existence and intelligibility of necessary logical, mathematical, and evidential conditions to the necessary God of Christian theism.

centralBridges.description: Show that reasoning already depends on invariant logic, stable meaning, interpersonal correspondence, and an intelligible reality requiring a worldview-level account.
Establish that necessary logical and mathematical truths are immaterial and require an absolute universal mind rather than merely contingent human descriptions.
Show that certainty about one's own existence does not by itself license conclusions about every possible world or universally normative logical principles.
Maintain the creator–creation and necessary–contingent distinctions needed to block transferring divine explanatory attributes directly to the cosmos.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish contingent linguistic expressions from the necessary truths they express so that descriptions are not conflated with their modal content.
Explain why evidential demands depend on antecedent conditions of intelligibility and therefore cannot be treated as worldview-neutral.

routes.description: Establish that immediate self-experience and reality itself provide a non-theistic basis for intelligibility, with logic, mathematics, and language functioning as derived descriptive systems rather than entities requiring a divine mind.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if self-existence supplies a secure epistemic starting point, objective identity and necessity obtain independently of divine propositions, and adding a sustaining or grounding God contributes no required explanatory condition.

motionBridge.description: Account for logic, mathematics, knowledge, and intelligible reality without requiring Christian theism as their precondition.

centralBridges.description: Ground the epistemic starting point in the impossibility of mistakenly believing that one exists and explain its relevance to logical reasoning.
Establish that reality cannot cease to be reality and that identity and related necessities hold regardless of reality's particular form.
Separate mind-dependent logical and mathematical sentences from the objective realities and relations they accurately describe.
Show that reality can persist by its own nature and that assigning persistence or necessity to God does not require inserting a separate divine sustainer.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish conclusions derived from experience from foundational presuppositions, including logic, mathematics, and linguistic concepts.
Explain why useful epistemic description and interaction need not await an ultimate intrinsic definition of matter or energy.

sections.title: Self-Experience and the Epistemic Starting Point
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether indubitable first-person existence can ground knowledge and logical reasoning without God, or whether an additional principle is required to reach objective and universally normative conclusions.

sections.title: From Identity to Modal and Temporal Necessity
sections.rationale: This section addresses how claims about self-identity and reality's identity extend across possible worlds and time, including the disputed bridge from immediate certainty to necessary logical structure.

sections.title: Necessary Truths, Descriptions, and Ontology
sections.rationale: The distinction between contingent symbols and necessarily accurate logical or mathematical content bears directly on whether such truths require an absolute mind or can describe reality without existing as divine mental objects.

sections.title: Presuppositions and the Intelligibility of Evidence
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether logic, language, correspondence, and evidence are conclusions available from experience or antecedent worldview conditions whose intelligibility requires Christian theism.

sections.title: Reality's Persistence and the Creator–Creation Distinction
sections.rationale: This section captures whether reality needs an external sustainer, whether divine explanatory attributes can be assigned directly to reality, and whether necessary God and contingent creation form a burden-relevant distinction.

routes.description: Establish that consciousness, a persisting personal subject, future-directed purpose, objective value, and genuine agency contain features that no exhaustive physical description can constitute or explain.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if at least one motion-level feature is shown to be real and indispensable to personhood while remaining neither identical with nor fully explicable through physical structure, computation, function, or causal history.

motionBridge.description: Show that one or more essential features of persons require an ontological or explanatory basis beyond an exhaustive inventory of physical facts.

centralBridges.description: Establish that first-person experience is a determinate fact whose existence and qualitative character are not exhausted by neural, behavioral, or functional descriptions.
Establish that unified experience, memory, anticipation, reasoning, and choice require a continuing subject that uses but is not identical with the brain.
Establish that intentional purposes, objective values, and controlled alternative possibilities have normative or causal roles unavailable to purposeless physical processes alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support irreducibility by distinguishing the brain's provision of access to consciousness from the production or exhaustive constitution of consciousness.
Require justification for treating an unfinished and conceptually unsettled naturalistic program as capable of explaining every feature named in the motion.

routes.description: Show that consciousness and personhood arise through evolved physical organization while purpose, value, identity, and responsible agency remain genuine at appropriate functional and higher explanatory levels.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic accounts accommodate the phenomena named in the motion without eliminating their practical significance and no additional nonphysical subject, property, purpose giver, or causal power is required.

motionBridge.description: Show that materially realized processes and legitimate higher-level explanations jointly account for persons without implying metaphysical ingredients beyond the natural world.

centralBridges.description: Explain conscious perspective and the apparent self through unconscious brain computation, responsiveness, and an evolved user interface without positing a separate inner observer.
Explain how purposeless evolution, prediction, and socially developed practices generate genuine purposes and discoverable or improvable values without top-down design.
Establish that autonomy, self-control, reasoning, and robust abilities ground responsibility even if underlying processes are deterministic, while indeterminacy supplies no added control.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve indispensable personal-level explanations of meaning, love, beauty, and agency while denying that explanatory autonomy entails metaphysical irreducibility.
Ground confidence in further naturalistic explanation in its empirical record and explanatory economy rather than an unsupported promise of completeness.

sections.title: Consciousness and Physical Description
sections.rationale: Tests whether experience is ontologically basic or an additional fact beyond physical description, against accounts based on unconscious computation, neural responsiveness, functional capacities, and the rejection of an inner show.

sections.title: Personal Identity, the Self, and Continuity
sections.rationale: Addresses whether memory, anticipation, unified awareness, embodiment, and informational continuity require a persisting nonphysical subject or can be explained by an evolved self-model and materially realized organization.

sections.title: Purpose, Intentionality, and Future Direction
sections.rationale: Examines whether future-directed thought and action possess irreducible aboutness and causal efficacy or arise through natural selection, predictive processing, and organized goal-directed capacities.

sections.title: Value, Meaning, and Higher-Level Explanation
sections.rationale: Determines whether objective obligation, beauty, love, and meaningful conduct require realities beyond a physical catalogue or remain genuine through evolved practices and autonomous higher-level explanations.

sections.title: Freedom, Agency, and Responsibility
sections.rationale: Compares libertarian control by a deciding self with compatibilist autonomy and robust abilities, including whether alternative futures are required for culpability and whether indeterminacy adds control rather than randomness.

sections.title: Reduction, Causation, and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: Assesses substrate dependence, brain access versus production, causal and functional sufficiency, the conceptual boundary of the physical, and the evidential warrant for expecting naturalistic explanation to cover the full motion.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Consciousness is ontologically prior, while the material world is constructed from conscious experience.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Keith to define idealism, and the uninterrupted answer presents his first-person account.

response.rationale: This constructive move directly proposes idealism as a motion-level account, claiming consciousness exists in its own right and matter is constructed from it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed responsivenessWithinClass values (86 and 83); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but the sense in which matter is a logical construction from consciousness is only partly specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A sweeping ontological conclusion is asserted from an idealist characterization without an argument excluding physicalist alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The position is internally intelligible, but the bridge from the priority of experience in presentation to ontological priority is undeveloped.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Scientific investigation indicates that conscious experience depends on complex unconscious computations in the brain, reversing the claim that experience is ontologically prior to the physical world.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Daniel for the naturalist account, and the ensuing sustained answer directly contrasts Keith's position.

components.text: The decisive demand is whether consciousness is ontologically prior rather than dependent on physical processes.

response.rationale: The reply directly counters priority by asserting that ordinary conscious experience depends on sophisticated unconscious brain computations, although dependence alone does not settle constitution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The dependence claim and its intended reversal are clear, with an implicit limitation to scientifically investigated human experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Brain dependence is plausibly asserted, but treating it as undermining idealism requires a further metaphysical premise not made explicit.

charity.alternative: Idealism can accept systematic brain dependence as the structure through which consciousness is accessed or organized.
charity.decisiveQualification: Empirical dependence does not by itself establish that brain computation produces or exhaustively constitutes experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unconscious computational dependence to rejection of ontological priority is plausible but contains a material unstated bridge.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Conscious awareness is an additional fact beyond any complete physical description because first-person experience remains directly known even while particular mental judgments can be fallible.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator names Keith and requests his objection; Ward then gives a sustained first-person response about brains and awareness.

components.text: Whether neural computational dependence exhausts the fact of directly known conscious awareness.

response.rationale: Ward contacts the computational account by distinguishing fallible judgments from directly known awareness and asserting that awareness remains additional to physical description.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the alleged explanatory remainder, though it does not fully show why direct knowledge entails nonphysical constitution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between fallible judgments and direct knowledge of being aware is clearly stated and appropriately qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges fallibility, but the move from direct awareness to being additional to every physical description remains somewhat overstated.

charity.alternative: A physicalist can accept direct first-person knowledge while identifying awareness with physically realized functional or neural states.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic directness and third-person descriptive difference do not alone entail ontological addition.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Positing consciousness beyond observable cognitive capacities repeats the discarded vitalist demand for an extra property beyond the processes that constitute life.
moves.attributionBasis: Following the moderator's request for a response, Dennett identifies Chalmers's formulation and argues against it in his own voice.

components.text: Whether an extra fact of consciousness must be added beyond all observable cognitive capacities.
Whether consciousness must be treated as an ontologically additional basis rather than a constituted capacity.

response.rationale: Dennett diagnoses the demand for an extra consciousness property as repeating vitalism and states that the proposed addition is detached from the capacities being explained.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply expressly attacks the extra-property inference, although the analogy does not independently prove that phenomenal experience is exhausted by capacities.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy is recoverable, but the alleged extra consciousness property and its relation to studied capacities are incompletely characterized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The analogy supplies a plausible diagnostic warning, but the suggestion that the two explanatory demands are equivalent is stronger than the excerpt establishes.

charity.alternative: The hard-problem claimant can argue that phenomenal character differs categorically from vitalism's proposed biological force.
charity.decisiveQualification: Explaining behavioral capacities may leave the asserted first-person qualitative fact untouched.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnostic analogy is coherent, but its force depends on an underdefended equivalence between life-process completeness and consciousness-capacity completeness.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The historical comparison is suggestive rather than demonstrative and offers little specific support that all relevant conscious facts track the studied capacities.

response.rationale: The access model directly contests the interpretation of brain dependence, but it does not answer the vitalism diagnostic or support the survival of inaccessible memories.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive production-versus-access issue but leaves the competing diagnostic and empirical discrimination substantially unanswered.

moves.proposition: Memory, anticipation, and the ownership of experience require a persisting subject that is embodied and uses the brain but is not identical with it.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator asks Ward about the soul, Ward gives an extended account of the subject that possesses temporally linked experiences.

Whether positing a persisting subject adds an unnecessary entity beyond cognitive capacities.

response.rationale: The move supplies a contrary subject-based account of temporal ownership but does not examine how computation might realize continuity or answer the redundancy objection.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity of a non-brain subject is asserted from temporal linkage without excluding materially realized continuity accounts.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Consciousness and the apparent self function as an evolved user interface that simplifies internal and external complexity without requiring a separate inner user.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator asks who uses the brain, and Dennett immediately answers that the brain is its own user before developing the interface model.

components.text: Whether using the brain requires a separate persisting inner subject that serves as its user.
Whether consciousness includes an additional fact beyond evolved functional organization.

response.rationale: Dennett answers that the brain is its own user and offers an evolved interface model, thereby contacting the separate-user, additional-fact, and access-machine claims.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Evolutionary design plausibly explains simplification, while identifying consciousness wholesale with the interface exceeds the supplied support somewhat.

charity.alternative: The pro side can accept an interface while maintaining that a real subject experiences or uses it.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: A wholly physical account cannot preserve genuine purpose because physical laws and atomic processes have no purposes of their own, making experienced aims merely illusory.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly challenges the preceding naturalistic account and consistently presents Ward's first-person objection to physical causation.

components.text: Whether a brain described as an evolved interface can possess genuine purposes rather than merely simulate them.
Whether purposeless neural and physical processes can preserve experienced aims as causally genuine.
Whether functional capacities exhaust the purposive features attributed to conscious agents.

response.rationale: Ward directly challenges the interface and physical accounts on purpose, arguing that purposeless laws and atoms cannot ground genuine aims, while leaving the functional-capacity reply undeveloped.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive purpose issue is contacted, but the move assumes rather than demonstrates that purposeless components cannot compose purposive systems.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clear, but purpose shifts between intrinsic aims of atoms, system-level goals, and first-person intentions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that physicalism necessarily loses purpose is stronger than the premise that physical laws and atoms lack purposes.

charity.alternative: Purposes may be genuine higher-level organizational properties even when elementary laws and particles lack purposes.
charity.decisiveQualification: Emergence requires explanation, but absence at the component level does not entail absence in organized systems.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Natural selection is a purposeless physical process that gradually creates genuine purposes in organisms, limbs, eyes, and tools without a top-down divine purpose giver.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly invokes Dennett's book and gives his characteristic Darwinian bottom-up explanation of purpose.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive premise and supplies a clear alternative generative direction from purposeless selection to purposive organization.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The confident claim fits the familiar explanatory role of selection, while the metaphysical sufficiency claim remains modestly implicit.

charity.alternative: The pro objection can distinguish selected biological function from conscious, reason-guided, or intrinsic purpose.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies natural selection as purposeless yet purpose-generating and applies the account to organisms, limbs, eyes, and tools.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Future-directed intentionality resists physical reduction because a present idea can refer to a nonexistent future outcome and causally guide action toward realizing it.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person argument follows Ward's stated rejection of Dennett's project and develops his intentionality objection.

components.text: Whether evolutionary organization can explain present representations that guide action toward future outcomes.
Whether an evolved interface can possess causally efficacious future-directed representations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move is relevant and contacts a secondary functional issue, while leaving the primary Darwinian generative explanation largely unexamined.

precisionFindings.rationale: The present-thought and future-outcome relation is clear, but the scope of the claimed failure of physical description is unspecified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the point partly as a difficulty, but still moves too quickly from future nonexistence to physical inexplicability.

moves.proposition: Objective moral obligations are discovered rather than invented, and their connection to purpose and agency places value outside an exhaustive physical catalogue.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Humanly constructed systems can contain discoverable constraints and opportunities for improvement, so evolved moral practices may support genuine moral discovery without requiring values external to nature.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly identifies Ward's position before answering through Darwinian predictive coding, chess, and cultural moral development.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Responsibility-relevant freedom consists in autonomy, self-control, and robust practical abilities, none of which requires the underlying physical world to be indeterministic.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett explicitly presents the compatibilist view, using autonomous systems, self-control, and the putting example to define relevant freedom.

components.text: Whether responsibility and agency require a nonphysical value-bearing chooser rather than autonomous control capacities.
Whether physically realized systems can possess genuine goal-directed control and purposes.
Whether practical abilities can guide future-directed conduct without indeterministic causation.

response.rationale: Dennett justifies replacing metaphysical indeterminism with the responsibility-relevant demand for autonomy, self-control, and robust abilities, preserving the practical agency issue.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe preserves control and responsibility while directly identifying the functional capacities that allegedly do the required work.

precisionFindings.rationale: Freedom is expressly specified as autonomy, control, and practical capacity rather than metaphysical indeterminacy.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is firmly advocated but appropriately tied to responsibility-relevant freedom, not every conceivable definition of metaphysical freedom.

charity.alternative: Libertarian freedom demands ultimate alternative possibilities, not merely autonomous abilities within a determined history.
charity.decisiveQualification: A compatibilist reframe must explain why robust control satisfies responsibility despite the absence of ultimate alternatives.

moves.speaker: Keith Ward
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom requires genuinely alternative futures under an agent's control, grounding culpability because the person need not have performed the wrongful act.
moves.attributionBasis: Ward identifies himself as a libertarian and develops the view through alternative futures, legal guilt, moral culpability, and Humean doubt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity of controlled alternatives for culpability is asserted with a clear rationale, but competing responsibility conditions are not fully excluded.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism grounds culpability in reasons-responsive control and robust abilities rather than identical-past alternative possibilities.
charity.decisiveQualification: A rewinding test may presuppose the disputed libertarian standard instead of refuting compatibilist control.

routes.description: Establish that belief in God supplies truth-grounded moral authority, purpose, human significance, and durable social commitments that secular reason and institutions cannot fully reproduce.
routes.successCriteria: Connect a credible transcendent account of reality to distinctive moral and social benefits, while showing that secular substitutes leave material gaps in obligation, meaning, solidarity, or confidence in humanity's future.

motionBridge.description: Show that the distinctive truth, moral, purposive, and communal functions of belief in God make people and societies better off overall.

centralBridges.description: Establish that morality requires a standard beyond prevailing consensus or self-interest to ground equal worth, prophetic criticism, and restraint of power.
Establish that a divinely ordered reality provides warranted purpose, human significance, and confidence in a shared future beyond material utility.
Establish that religious belief sustains forms of community and institutional commitment that secular civic or governmental substitutes do not fully preserve.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why inherited belief, religious disagreement, and scientific revision do not preclude rational commitment to fundamental religious truth claims.
Identify limits or tensions in naturalistic accounts of reason, consciousness, moral knowledge, and humanity's distinctive intellectual capacities.

routes.description: Establish that reason centered on human flourishing can ground morality, knowledge, purpose, and cooperation, while secular institutions can preserve beneficial social practices without theological commitments.
routes.successCriteria: Provide workable secular foundations for moral obligation and reliable knowledge, connect them to effective institutions and historical progress, and show that religion's beneficial components are separable from disputed doctrines.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular reason and institutions can provide morality, purpose, knowledge, and social cooperation at least as effectively without requiring belief in God.

centralBridges.description: Ground moral duties and equal rights in impartial consistency, reciprocal concern, conscious interests, agency, and the shared gains from cooperative conduct.
Establish empirical testing, correction, and information-processing explanations as sufficient foundations for reliable knowledge without supernatural premises.
Establish that public welfare, civic association, democracy, and universal human-rights institutions can deliver cooperation and moral progress at broad scale.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate religion's community, ritual, music, and fellowship from theological, repressive, or obsolete claims so beneficial practices can be retained selectively.
Require causal evidence before attributing well-being, cohesion, polarization, or historical violence to either religious belief or secularization.

sections.title: Foundations of morality, obligation, and equal worth
sections.rationale: The motion centrally turns on whether transcendent authority is needed to justify duties, protect equal human value, criticize accepted injustice, and restrain conduct that benefits powerful actors.

sections.title: Community, welfare, and institutional cooperation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether religion provides distinctive and durable social attachment or whether civic organizations, public programs, and selectively preserved communal practices can perform the relevant functions.

sections.title: Reason, religious truth, and naturalistic explanation
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of reliable knowledge determine whether belief in God is rationally warranted and whether evolution, scientific correction, cognition, and consciousness can be explained within a secular framework.

sections.title: Historical violence, institutional failure, and moral progress
sections.rationale: Claims about totalitarianism, religious complicity, institutional recovery, democracy, and human rights bear on which worldview can support stable improvement rather than merely inherit or cause social failures.

sections.title: Purpose, human significance, and confidence in the future
sections.rationale: The debate also requires comparing the resources of theistic and secular worldviews for sustaining personal meaning, human distinctiveness, social hope, and commitment to future generations.

moves.speaker: Ross Douthat
moves.proposition: Belief in God roots morality, human value, reason, and purpose in fundamental realities about the universe, while religious decline contributes to polarization and purposelessness.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Douthat the floor, and he delivers an uninterrupted opening argument through his concluding thanks.

response.rationale: This opening constructively states the theistic route by connecting God to morality, value, reason, purpose, and claimed social consequences; it has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it supplies a broad, clearly organized route touching several indispensable motion-level functions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The main thesis is recoverable, but “fundamental realities,” cultural benefit, polarization, and purposelessness cover several distinct causal and metaphysical claims without stable limits.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling God's existence self-evident and linking religious decline to broad social maladies asserts substantially more than the excerpt's compressed support establishes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is intelligible, but it compresses the bridges from God's existence to grounded values and from religious decline to contemporary social outcomes.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The adjudicated raw ledger applies the preregistered rounded mean to the two nondisputed evidenceWarrant values (57 and 58); their difference did not meet a semantic or magnitude dispute trigger.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, the move expressly advances the overall claim that cultures are better off when rooted in belief in God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The opening presents its positive worldview rather than developing a meaningful competing interpretation that can be tested for charitable treatment.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly calls God self-evidently real, treats rootedness in that reality as good, and links the claim to morality, reason, purpose, and culture.

moves.speaker: Steven Pinker
moves.proposition: Shared human interests provide a common mission in which science, knowledge, and reason are applied to reduce suffering, enhance flourishing, and achieve measurable human progress without reliance on God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator names Pinker and reverses the opening question; Pinker then gives a sustained answer ending with an explicit conclusion and thanks.

components.text: Whether purpose and a shared human mission require grounding in God rather than common human interests.
Whether secular reason can generate measurable improvements in suffering, flourishing, and social progress.
Whether secular resources fully answer the opening claim about objective human value and fundamental reality.

response.rationale: The reply directly offers common human interests and demonstrated progress as a secular source of mission, but it does not fully answer the distinct metaphysical grounding claim about objective value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a strong partial answer because it contacts the decisive practical-purpose component while leaving the distinct reality-grounding component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The secular mission and outcome test are clear, though the broad attribution of multiple historical gains to human reason leaves institutional and causal scope partly compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The cited trends support substantial progress, but “no thanks to God” and the general causal attribution exceed what those aggregate examples alone establish.

routes.description: Establish the Kalam conclusion by defending a cause for anything that begins, showing that a concrete infinite past and its successive formation are impossible, and connecting the universe's finite beginning to a transcendent personal cause.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the causal principle applies to the universe, the philosophical arguments establish a finite past, and conceptual analysis supports a first cause with the power and agency required to originate a temporal universe.

motionBridge.description: Connect the defended causal premise and finite-past premise to a caused beginning of the universe and then to a personal creator.

centralBridges.description: Require a noncircular justification for applying the principle that whatever begins to exist has a cause to an absolute cosmic beginning.
Require the actual-infinite and successive-addition arguments to exclude a beginningless sequence of past events.
Require the inferred first cause to account for a finite temporal effect in a way that supports power, transcendence, and personal agency.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the absence of anything from an entity called nothing while preserving the claimed need for a cause without a material source.
Use part-whole, subtraction, countdown, and non-well-founded sequence cases to support the premises excluding an infinite past.

routes.description: Block the Kalam conclusion by challenging the extension of ordinary causal reasoning to all material reality, preserving the coherence of a beginningless past, and showing that a first cause would not by itself entail a powerful timeless personal creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a material beginning is not shown to require a cause, the arguments against an actual or successively realized infinite past remain inconclusive, or the inferred cause lacks a warranted path to the creator attributes stated in the motion.

motionBridge.description: Connect failures in either Kalam premise or in the conceptual analysis of a first cause to the motion's complete conjunctive claim.

centralBridges.description: Require independent support for extending causal judgments about rearrangements of prior material to the categorically different beginning of all material reality.
Require the alleged absurdities and formation objections to establish impossibility rather than merely counterintuitive features of infinite collections or histories.
Require the first-cause conclusion to exclude weaker, mediated, impersonal, indeterministic, or nonconscious alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Prevent grammatical references to nothing from supplying an entity, nature, power, or discriminatory capacity that could support the causal premise.
Test whether local predecessor and rate facts can explain stages of a beginningless sequence without an unrestricted principle of sufficient reason.

sections.title: Causal Principle, Material Beginning, and Nothing
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether ordinary caused beginnings support a universal causal premise and whether an absolute material beginning requires a cause without reifying nothing.

sections.title: Concrete Actual Infinities and Metaphysical Impossibility
sections.rationale: This issue covers whether Hilbert-style part-whole and subtraction cases establish that a concrete actual infinite is impossible rather than merely unusual.

sections.title: Successive Formation and a Beginningless Past
sections.rationale: This issue tests the independent route from successive addition, countdown timing, local explanation, and non-well-founded sequences to a finite past.

sections.title: Power and the Structure of the First Cause
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether the universe's magnitude and the termination of intermediate causal chains warrant the claimed power and ultimacy of its first cause.

sections.title: Personhood, Indeterminism, and Timeless Consciousness
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether a finite temporal effect specifically requires personal agency and whether timeless changeless personhood is coherent relative to impersonal alternatives.

routes.description: Establish that action necessarily expresses a highest-order value structure, that the West's operative structure is substantially inherited through religious narratives and institutions, and that this inheritance supplies indispensable resources for morality, meaning, suffering, and social coordination.
routes.successCriteria: Show that secular professions and practices do not constitute a self-sufficient replacement because coherent conduct, durable ethics, and tragedy-sustaining meaning continue to depend on functions performed by God, religious stories, or religiously inherited values.

motionBridge.description: Connect the unavoidable requirements of coherent action, moral order, and meaning under suffering to God, religious narrative, or inherited religious values.

centralBridges.description: Establish that conduct embodies a hierarchy of values whose highest commitment performs the functional role attributed to God.
Explain why secular morality and institutions remain dependent on inherited commitments such as individual sovereignty and truthful speech.
Show why religious narratives provide meaning capable of organizing action through unavoidable tragedy and human malevolence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Ground religious archetypes and ethical patterns in culturally and biologically deep structures of adaptive conduct.
Account for the vacuum and destabilizing substitutes that may follow removal of inherited religious foundations.

routes.description: Establish that biological and memetic evolution can explain religion, morality, and higher meanings without divine grounding, while secular reflection, contemplative practice, and ordinary social life can sustain motivation, gratitude, ethical conduct, and acceptance of suffering.
routes.successCriteria: Provide a sufficient secular account of meaning and morality, distinguish religious usefulness from religious necessity or divine truth, and show that functioning persons and societies can relinquish God without the predicted collapse into nihilism or disorder.

motionBridge.description: Demonstrate that humans can make sense of action, morality, suffering, and meaning through secular evolutionary, cultural, and experiential resources.

centralBridges.description: Explain religious persistence and higher meaning through distinct biological and cultural replication processes without requiring divine causation.
Show how secular reflection, meditation, evolved motivation, and social life can support gratitude, ethical conduct, and purposeful action.
Use secular persons and societies as counterexamples to claims that abandoning God necessarily produces moral or social collapse.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate the practical wisdom or social benefits of religious traditions from claims of divine causation, guilt, or necessity.
Require an explanation of prosocial atheist conduct that does not redefine all moral behavior as implicitly religious.

sections.title: Belief, conduct, and the functional meaning of God
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether every coherent value hierarchy is properly understood as religious and whether moral atheist conduct confirms that thesis or supplies a secular counterexample.

sections.title: Secular ethics, stable societies, and religious inheritance
sections.rationale: The necessity claim turns substantially on whether morality and stable institutions can stand independently or remain downstream of inherited religious commitments and vulnerable when those foundations recede.

sections.title: Evolutionary archetypes, memes, and religious persistence
sections.rationale: Competing biological and cultural explanations bear on whether religious patterns encode indispensable realities of successful conduct or persist as historically contingent, independently copied complexes.

sections.title: Religious and secular responses to tragedy and ultimate meaning
sections.rationale: Because the motion expressly concerns suffering and life's meaning, this section tests whether religious stories uniquely sustain action through tragedy or whether acceptance of cosmic pointlessness remains compatible with positive living.

sections.title: Secular gratitude and the construction of higher meaning
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether gratitude and coordinated higher-order meaning require an implicit divine object or can emerge through contemplative practice, evolved needs, and memetic cultural construction.

moves.speaker: Jordan Peterson

routes.description: Establish Christianity as the better moral foundation for society by connecting its truth claims and account of transcendent moral obligation to universal human dignity, protection of vulnerable people, and durable practices of sacrificial community and social flourishing.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by explaining why Christian claims furnish an objective and socially actionable moral ground, why the incarnation and cross support equal dignity beyond contingent human preference, and why secular humanism cannot secure the same protections or benefits on its own premises.

motionBridge.description: Show that Christianity provides society a more secure and beneficial moral foundation than atheism or secular humanism.

centralBridges.description: Connect objective moral values and obligations to a true transcendent foundation that cannot be reduced to biology, preference, or social agreement.
Explain how divine identification with vulnerable humanity grounds equal dignity and protection even when human interests narrow the moral circle.
Connect intrinsic Christian commitment with durable communal practices and social benefits not fully explained by community participation alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for the persistence of sacred values and exclusionary group dynamics within nominally irreligious communities.
Explain Christianity's claimed historical role in forming norms of sacrifice by the strong for weak people and outsiders.

routes.description: Establish secular humanism as the better moral foundation for society by distinguishing it from bare atheism, grounding deliberation in shared human interests and well-being, and showing that community, moral revision, and protection from harm do not require supernatural premises.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by presenting a usable human-centered standard for moral evaluation, showing how secular communities can reproduce relevant social goods, answering claims that dignity or obligation requires God, and demonstrating comparative advantages from revising harmful inherited doctrines.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular humanism offers society a more workable and corrigible moral foundation than Christianity while bare atheism need not supply a complete program.

centralBridges.description: Ground moral deliberation in shared concern for human beings and assess conduct through consequences for human well-being.
Show that invoking God neither resolves motivational disagreement nor establishes the truth or practical accessibility of the proposed moral foundation.
Explain how secular humanism can inherit useful traditions while correcting doctrines or practices that conflict with present human flourishing.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that secular communities can sustain belonging, awe, higher commitments, sacrifice, and practical support without supernatural belief.
Explain how consequence-based moral reasoning can remain revisable while still criticizing exclusionary and oppressive social systems.

sections.title: Foundation, Truth, and Moral Objectivity
sections.rationale: The central metaphysical clash concerns whether moral truth and obligation require a nonmaterial Christian explanation or can begin from human interests without an additional divine premise.

sections.title: Human Dignity and the Moral Circle
sections.rationale: The comparative burdens turn substantially on whether universal protection for weak and excluded people is secured by divine identification with humanity or by human valuation and shared well-being.

sections.title: Community, Transcendence, and Social Flourishing
sections.rationale: Claims about health, resilience, generosity, belonging, awe, and higher commitments test whether Christianity supplies distinctive social goods or whether secular institutions can reproduce their operative causes.

sections.title: Moral Inheritance, Revision, and Social Consequences
sections.rationale: The motion requires comparing Christianity's claimed historical formation of humane norms with secular humanism's capacity to preserve useful ideas, reject harmful baggage, and revise judgments through their consequences.

sections.title: Atheism, Secular Humanism, and Public Practice
sections.rationale: Distinguishing bare atheism from secular humanism and examining disagreement, dogmatism, and shared premises determines what each position actually proposes as a workable social foundation.
